MECHANISM: A sharp transition into unusually high option-implied fear can coincide with forced de-risking, convexity hedging and liquidity demand. If part of that demand is temporary, the broad equity index can rebound over the next several sessions. If fear is correctly pricing a persistent deterioration, the contrarian expression should fail and may carry crash risk.
WHO_PAYS: Potentially investors forced to sell/de-risk or buy protection during acute fear episodes; positive subsequent equity returns may also simply compensate crash/liquidity risk rather than reveal mispricing.
WHY_PERSIST: Risk limits, margin/liquidity constraints and convexity demand recur, while the exact timing of reversals is difficult and dangerous to warehouse. Publication/crowding makes a large simple effect unlikely.
OBSERVABLE_TRIGGER: CBOE VIX daily close entering an extreme tail relative only to its own trailing history, with equity entry strictly after the signal close.
CHEAP_DATA_NOW: FRED exposes VIXCLS (daily VIX close, source CBOE) and SP500 (daily S&P 500 close). Both routes are public, no account and no paid service required for this bounded research screen.
CHEAP_EXPRESSION: When VIX first crosses into the top 5% of its trailing 252 valid closes, take one non-overlapping paper LONG S&P 500 proxy from the next available close for five subsequent closes. Threshold, horizon and costs must be frozen before joined historical outcomes are read.
WHY_NOT_ARBITRAGED: Not established. VIX spikes and equity rebounds are widely studied; any apparent return may be compensation for crash risk, a sample dominated by crisis episodes, or a non-executable close-to-close artifact.
FATAL_PROBLEM: Signals cluster in crises, observations are dependent, and extreme-VIX episodes can precede much deeper equity losses. Using same-day SP500 close would create timing ambiguity, so entry must be strictly after the VIX signal close. Cash-index closes are not executable futures fills.
